steps.html:
Charge polluting cars more to park, and you will hear every kind of disagreement in about ninety seconds. Then a film about laws so strange that people refuse to believe they are real — and some of them are not.

  • Follow a three-way argument and hear who is on whose side
  • Agree and disagree strongly, and know how strong you sound
  • Watch a documentary about laws and how they get interpreted
  • Write a for-and-against paragraph and a persuasive letter

steps.title: Before you listen: whose side would you be on?

The person with an old car who can't afford a new one

steps.title: Listen. What is the proposal being discussed?
options: Parking will be free for everyone in the city centre.
The more pollution your car causes, the more you pay to park.
Only electric cars will be allowed to park.
steps.answer: The more pollution your car causes, the more you pay to park.
steps.why: 'The more pollution your car causes, the more you pay.'

steps.title: Listen again. True or false?

steps.why: 'My car is quite old, so I'll have to pay more. I can't afford to buy a new car.'

steps.title: Listen again. True or false?
steps.prompt: Speaker C agrees with speaker A.
steps.why: 'I'm with you there' is said to B — C thinks everyone should pay the same.

steps.title: Listen again. True or false?
steps.prompt: Speaker A suggests people could simply use their cars less.
steps.why: 'Or maybe you should just use your cars less in the first place?'

steps.title: Listen again. True or false?
steps.prompt: The discussion ends politely.
steps.why: It ends with 'Come off it! You use your car all the time' — the strongest disagreement in the clip.

steps.title: Listen once more.
steps.prompt: What is speaker B's argument, in one line?
options: Pollution is not a real problem.
A charge based on pollution punishes people for being poor.
Parking should be free for everyone.
steps.answer: A charge based on pollution punishes people for being poor.
steps.why: B's point is that the people with the oldest, dirtiest cars are the people who cannot afford to replace them.

steps.title: Read between the lines.
steps.sub: Speaker B says the car is old, that a new one is unaffordable, and asks how it is fair to pay more for parking as well.
steps.prompt: What is B's real objection to the charge?
options: That pollution from older cars has been exaggerated by the council.
That the charge falls hardest on the people least able to escape it, so it works as a tax on being poor.
That parking should be free everywhere in the city centre.
steps.answer: That the charge falls hardest on the people least able to escape it, so it works as a tax on being poor.
steps.why: B never disputes that the older car pollutes more. The argument is about who ends up paying, which is a different claim.

steps.title: Language noticing.
steps.sub: A replies with 'You can't be serious!' and B answers 'Come off it!'
steps.prompt: What do these two phrases tell you about the relationship between the speakers?
options: They are strangers, and the discussion has become hostile.
They know each other well enough to disagree bluntly without the conversation breaking down.
One of them is senior to the other and is using that position.
steps.answer: They know each other well enough to disagree bluntly without the conversation breaking down.
steps.why: Both phrases are informal and quite strong. You would not use either with somebody you had just met, and neither speaker treats them as an insult.

steps.title: How modals carry the weight of an argument
steps.html:
Nothing new here — the forms from Lessons 5 and 6, doing the work they were built for.

An argument is mostly modals. You state what people must or should do, what they shouldn't have to do, and what your opponent's position can't mean.

Obligation and prohibition set out the proposal: Drivers should pay more. Nobody should have to choose between food and parking. You mustn't punish people for being poor.

Deduction attacks the other side's reasoning: They can't have looked at the figures. The council must have known this would happen. Notice that can't have is doing the work of 'that is simply not credible'.

One structure carries a lot of B2 argument: shouldn't have to — 'this obligation is unfair'. Compare You shouldn't park here (advice) with You shouldn't have to pay to park here (protest).

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Ten sentences you can lift straight into a letter of protest.

Everyone should have to pay the same for the same service.
Speaker C's argument, almost word for word.

People shouldn't have to replace a working car to afford a parking space.
Objecting to an unfair obligation.

The council must publish the figures before the vote.
Insisting.

They can't have consulted anyone who drives an older car.
Deduction used as attack.

You may be right that pollution is the bigger problem, but…
Concede first, then push back.

Drivers of hybrids needn't pay anything under the scheme.
No obligation.

We mustn't let this become a charge on the poorest households.
Prohibition, used rhetorically.

Something must have changed since the consultation.
Certainty about the past.

There ought to be an exemption for anyone on a low income.
Proposal.

They might have meant it well, but the effect is the opposite.
Possibility + concession.

steps.title: Building one paragraph of an argument
steps.html:
1. Take the position: the charge is unfair to people with old cars.
  2. Open by conceding something, so you sound reasonable: The council may be right that pollution has to fall.
  3. State the objection as an unfair obligation: But nobody should have to replace a working car in order to park near their own home.
  4. Attack the reasoning with a deduction: They can't have looked at who actually drives the oldest cars in this borough.
  5. Close with your proposal: There ought to be an exemption for households below a set income. Four modals, four different jobs, one paragraph.

steps.title: What is the film's closing position?
options: Most laws are absurd and should be repealed.
In a world full of laws and regulations, common sense still has to do some of the work.
Only lawyers can ever know what is legal.
steps.answer: In a world full of laws and regulations, common sense still has to do some of the work.
steps.why: The final line is that it can be difficult to know what is illegal and what isn't — so sometimes we simply need a little common sense.

steps.title: Write a for-and-against paragraph.
steps.sub: 100–130 words on the parking proposal: the more your car pollutes, the more you pay. One paragraph for, one against, then one line saying where you stand.
steps.placeholder: Start with the case for, in your own words.
steps.html:
• Paragraph 1: the case for. Two reasons, not one, each with its own support.
  • Paragraph 2: the case against. Use <i>shouldn't have to</i> at least once.
  • Paragraph 3: deal with the strongest objection to your own position.
  • One closing line: where you stand and on what condition.

Useful language

  • The strongest argument in favour is that …
  • It could also be said that …
  • Against that, opponents point out that …
  • Nobody should have to …
  • They can't have considered …
  • On balance, I would argue that …
steps.modelHtml:
For. The strongest argument in favour is that a charge is the only measure that changes behaviour on the day it is introduced. Campaigns ask; parking meters decide. It could also be said that drivers of cleaner cars have already paid, in the price of the car, for the air everyone breathes.

Against. Against that, opponents point out that the oldest and dirtiest cars belong to the people with the least money. Nobody should have to replace a working vehicle in order to park near their own home, and a council that sets the charge without an income exemption can't have thought about who actually pays it.

On balance, I would support the charge, but only with an exemption below a set income.

steps.title: Now write the persuasive letter.
steps.sub: 160–190 words to your local council, arguing for or against the scheme. Formal register — none of the strong informal phrases from the recording.
steps.html:
• Open with your purpose in one sentence.
  • Concede something real before you object.
  • State your objection as an unfair obligation.
  • Attack one specific weakness in the proposal, with a deduction.
  • Close with a single concrete request and a formal sign-off.

Useful language

  • I am writing to ask you to reconsider …
  • While I accept that …, I would argue that …
  • The proposal appears to prohibit … from …
  • Residents should not have to …
  • I would urge the council to introduce an exemption for …
  • I look forward to your reply. Yours faithfully, …
steps.modelHtml:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to ask you to reconsider the proposed pollution-based parking charges in the borough.

While I accept that air quality must improve, and that the council is under real pressure on public spending, I would argue that this scheme places the cost on precisely the households least able to carry it. The oldest and most polluting vehicles on our streets belong to people who cannot replace them. Residents should not have to give up a working car in order to park outside their own homes.

The consultation document estimates a ten per cent fall in traffic. It contains no assessment of who will pay. The council can't have examined the income profile of the affected streets, or that assessment would appear somewhere in the document.

I would urge you to introduce an exemption for households below a set income before the scheme begins.

I look forward to your reply.

Yours faithfully,
